claims.assertion: The GPS track shows one off-route segment (22:57–23:01) covering 2.19 km where the optimal route covers 1.38 km, adding 0.80 km and straying up to 1014 m from the optimal route; under RD-1 this unexcused deviation breaches the driver's obligation to take the shortest and most direct route.

The trip was driven on RydeTAXI, a metered service, so the 0.80 km of unexcused extra distance entered the meter: the fare scaled at $1.41/km (F4, F6), and RD-2 entitles the rider to a partial refund of the unexcused segment's extra km at that per-km rate, i.e. 0.80 × $1.41 = $1.13 (rounded to the cent).

The driver's own statement — 'Ayer Rajah Expressway was crawling, so I went round it' — is an admission he left the optimal route without asking the rider first; no chat message before 22:57 shows any proposed route change or rider agreement, and the only pre-trip messages concern the meeting point.

The driver's congestion excuse fails RD-4: there is no traffic incident recorded near the route during the trip window (F13), and the only congestion band evidence on the optimal route is at 300 m matching radius, whereas RD-4(b) band data alone does not excuse a segment; the rider's route deviation is therefore unexcused.

Because RD-2 yields a refund greater than zero on this deviation, the driver's 90-day profile (3 disputes, 1 upheld) supplies the additional ground for a flag_account referral to Ryde account review under RD-6; the profile is cited only as an add-on action, not as the finding itself.

weaknesses: The total excess billed is only partly attributable to the single off-route segment: F1 shows +1.6 km overall while F3 attributes just 0.80 km to the detected deviation, so the remaining 0.8 km is map-matching residual / unsegmented excess that RD-2 says is not refundable — the driver will argue the whole +1.6 km / $2.33 (F4) should be excluded.

The driver will argue RD-4 reasonable cause using F10 (AYER RAJAH EXPRESSWAY speed band 1, 0–9 km/h, 22:39–22:57) and F11 (CENTRAL EXPRESSWAY band 1 through 23:15) as evidence of severe congestion on the optimal corridor, plus F14 light rain; we must show those band records do not meet RD-4(a) because F13 records no traffic incident on the optimal route.

This is a RydeTAXI metered fare, so the rider's framing ('the app estimated 11 km') does not control the fare; RD-0/RD-2 means only meter-derived distance excess is refundable, and the base/time/platform components of the $28.48 (F6) are not in dispute.

The driver's written statement (F9) post-dates the deviation, which cuts both ways: it is an admission of rerouting, but it also shows he announced a reason rather than riding in silence, which the judge may weigh as a partial justification.

events.body:

[F3 F10 F13] [RD-4]

→ D4: Conceded in part: no incident exists (F13), so the only possible exemption is the band record — and RD-4(b) expressly states band evidence is not sufficient on its own, so the 0.80 km segment (F3) stays unexempt and $1.13 (0.80 × $1.41/km, F4) is refundable under RD-2. [F3 F4 F13] [RD-4 RD-2]

points.response: The existence of the segment is not in dispute — F3 records it — but RD-1 defines an unexempted segment only after RD-3/RD-4/RD-5 review, and here the segment is supported by the recorded severe congestion on the substituted optimal route (F10: AYE band 1, 0–9 km/h, 22:39–22:57), so it is not an 'unexcused' deviation as C1 asserts.

Even on the rider's own arithmetic the recoverable figure is small and must be confined to the single segment: F3 attributes only 0.80 km to the segment while F1 shows +1.6 km total, and RD-2 expressly refuses the residual (the difference between fare-excess and the sum of segments, ≤ 0.25 km map-matching residual), so at most 0.80 × $1.41 = $1.13 is computable from F4 — and that amount falls away once the segment is exempt.

claims.assertion: The GPS track shows one off-route segment (22:57–23:01) covering 2.19 km where the optimal route covers 1.38 km, adding 0.80 km and straying up to 1014 m from the optimal route; under RD-1 this unexcused deviation breaches the driver's obligation to take the shortest and most direct route.

The trip was driven on RydeTAXI, a metered service, so the 0.80 km of unexcused extra distance entered the meter: the fare scaled at $1.41/km (F4, F6), and RD-2 entitles the rider to a partial refund of the unexcused segment's extra km at that per-km rate, i.e. 0.80 × $1.41 = $1.13 (rounded to the cent).

The driver's own statement — 'Ayer Rajah Expressway was crawling, so I went round it' — is an admission he left the optimal route without asking the rider first; no chat message before 22:57 shows any proposed route change or rider agreement, and the only pre-trip messages concern the meeting point.

The driver's congestion excuse fails RD-4: there is no traffic incident recorded near the route during the trip window (F13), and the only congestion band evidence on the optimal route is at 300 m matching radius, whereas RD-4(b) band data alone does not excuse a segment; the rider's route deviation is therefore unexcused.

Because RD-2 yields a refund greater than zero on this deviation, the driver's 90-day profile (3 disputes, 1 upheld) supplies the additional ground for a flag_account referral to Ryde account review under RD-6; the profile is cited only as an add-on action, not as the finding itself.

weaknesses: The total excess billed is only partly attributable to the single off-route segment: F1 shows +1.6 km overall while F3 attributes just 0.80 km to the detected deviation, so the remaining 0.8 km is map-matching residual / unsegmented excess that RD-2 says is not refundable — the driver will argue the whole +1.6 km / $2.33 (F4) should be excluded.

The driver will argue RD-4 reasonable cause using F10 (AYER RAJAH EXPRESSWAY speed band 1, 0–9 km/h, 22:39–22:57) and F11 (CENTRAL EXPRESSWAY band 1 through 23:15) as evidence of severe congestion on the optimal corridor, plus F14 light rain; we must show those band records do not meet RD-4(a) because F13 records no traffic incident on the optimal route.

This is a RydeTAXI metered fare, so the rider's framing ('the app estimated 11 km') does not control the fare; RD-0/RD-2 means only meter-derived distance excess is refundable, and the base/time/platform components of the $28.48 (F6) are not in dispute.

The driver's written statement (F9) post-dates the deviation, which cuts both ways: it is an admission of rerouting, but it also shows he announced a reason rather than riding in silence, which the judge may weigh as a partial justification.

claims.assertion: The single GPS-measured off-route segment is 22:57–23:01, 2.19 km driven where the optimal route covers 1.38 km, adding 0.80 km; this is the only deviation segment in the trip record.
The driver's explanation for the reroute is severe congestion on the Ayer Rajah Expressway, which is corroborated by the system record: AYE speed band 1 (0–9 km/h) during 22:39–22:57.

The congestion band covering the AYE ended at 22:57, the same minute the off-route segment began, so the recorded road state at the moment of the reroute decision supports the driver's account of avoiding the jam.

No traffic incident is recorded near the route during the trip window, so the exemption must rest on the speed-band record; the band record for the substituted optimal route shows severe congestion (band 1).

The parallel arterial the driver fell back on, Kent Ridge Road, was flowing at band 4 (30–39 km/h) over 22:39–23:15, i.e. the diversion produced a working alternative rather than an unexplained detour.
Weather fact (light rain, 1.8 mm) is consistent with the congestion on the AYE and supports the driver's account of not being able to proceed at normal speed.
The chat record contains no statement in which the driver refuses, or misrepresents, a routing request; the only driver message is an arrival notice, and the rider lodged no routing request in chat.

Because the off-route segment is exempt under the reasonable-cause exception, no amount is refundable on it: on this RydeTAXI trip the purely attributable excess is at most $2.33 (1.6 km × $1.41/km), and the exempt segment accounts for 0.80 km of it.
The fare breakdown contains no undocumented add-on: waiting $0.00, platform $1.47 (a published item), no surge (1.0×), and the meter components are base $3.90 + distance $17.50 + time $5.61 = $28.48.
The driver's 90-day record shows 1 upheld dispute with 0 route deviations upheld, so the 'repeated route deviation' condition for an account flag is not met.
The rider's own profile shows 2 disputes in 90 days and 0 upheld, i.e. no established pattern of driver misconduct behind this complaint.

weaknesses: RD-4(b) only makes a speed band corroborative: the policy says a band alone is 'not sufficient for exemption pending Ryde confirmation' (vacancy G3), and there is no traffic incident (F13), so the other side will argue the 0.80 km segment (F3) stays unexempt and $1.13 (0.80 km × $1.41/km, F4) should be refunded under RD-2.

The driver notified the rider only after the fact — chat contains no message asking permission for the routing change (F7, F8, F9) — so RD-5 consent cannot be argued, and RD-3(b) does not help since no stop was requested.

The trip ran +1.6 km and +4.3 min over estimate (F1, F2) while congestion is recorded ending at 22:57 (F10) and no incident existed (F13), so the rider can argue the deviation continued beyond the justified window and the reroute therefore was not purely the traffic situation.
The driver's own 90-day history contains 1 upheld dispute (F16); although it is 0 route cases, a judge may still treat the profile as an aggravating signal under RD-6.

points.response: Accepted as to the GPS measurement: F3 shows a single off-route segment 22:57–23:01 adding 0.80 km, and that segment is the basis of my RD-2 claim, not the driver's excuse for it.

The AYE band record (F10) does not corroborate this reroute under RD-4, because the deviation track runs 22:57–23:01 (F3) while the AYE band 1 window closes at 22:57 and RD-4(a) requires an incident located on the substituted optimal route, which F13 shows does not exist here.

Their own timing point defeats them: congestion ending at 22:57 (F10) cannot justify a diversion driven 22:57–23:01 (F3) over 2.19 km, and even if it did, a speed band alone is only corroborative and never exempts a segment under RD-4(b).

Conceded in part: no incident exists (F13), so the only possible exemption is the band record — and RD-4(b) expressly states band evidence is not sufficient on its own, so the 0.80 km segment (F3) stays unexempt and $1.13 (0.80 × $1.41/km, F4) is refundable under RD-2.

A route the driver never proposed to the rider cannot be legitimised by its own speed: RD-5 requires the driver to reach agreement before leaving the optimal route, and nothing in chats #1–#2 or the driver's statement (F7, F8, F9) seeks that agreement.

Light rain of 1.8 mm (F14) is not a traffic fact within RD-4's list and, like the band record, is not an accepted ground for exemption; only an incident on the optimal route under RD-4(a) exempts, and F13 confirms there was none.

Their point is correct but irrelevant: the rider made no routing request, which means RD-3 never engaged, and the rider's failure to request a route cannot excuse the driver's unauthorised deviation under RD-1.

Their own arithmetic concedes the segment: they measure 0.80 km of the excess on the 22:57–23:01 diversion (F3) at the $1.41/km rate (F4), which under RD-2 is exactly the refundable mileage, and my claim is limited to that $1.13 rather than the full $2.33.
This concerns FARE-1, which I did not contest: my claim is the RD-2 mileage refund of the unexempt segment (F3, F4), and the platform and base components of the $28.48 (F6) are not in dispute.

Conceded: F16 shows 0 route deviations upheld in the last 90 days, so RD-6's 'repeated route deviation' condition is not met and I withdraw the flag_account request; the finding and refund rest on F3 and F4 under RD-1/RD-2 alone.
My client's profile (F15) is not cited in my brief at all and cannot decide anything under RD-6; the refund stands or falls on the GPS segment F3, the fare rate F4 and the absence of an incident F13.
Withdrawn as conceded by the opponent's D10: F16 shows no upheld route deviation in 90 days, so RD-6 does not apply and no account flag is requested.

The existence of the segment is not in dispute — F3 records it — but RD-1 defines an unexempted segment only after RD-3/RD-4/RD-5 review, and here the segment is supported by the recorded severe congestion on the substituted optimal route (F10: AYE band 1, 0–9 km/h, 22:39–22:57), so it is not an 'unexcused' deviation as C1 asserts.

Even on the rider's own arithmetic the recoverable figure is small and must be confined to the single segment: F3 attributes only 0.80 km to the segment while F1 shows +1.6 km total, and RD-2 expressly refuses the residual (the difference between fare-excess and the sum of segments, ≤ 0.25 km map-matching residual), so at most 0.80 × $1.41 = $1.13 is computable from F4 — and that amount falls away once the segment is exempt.

The rider concedes there was no pre-trip agreement, but RD-5 is only one route to exemption and its absence does not decide the case; the rider's own message (F7) contains no routing instruction and no objection, and the driver's statement (F9) gave a reason contemporaneous with the manoeuvre rather than after the trip, which is the 'reasonable cause' that RD-4 governs.

RD-4's text makes the incident test (a) and the band test (b) alternatives, and F13's silence on incidents does not erase the band-1 record; RD-4(b) does not say band evidence is irrelevant, only that standalone sufficiency is pending Ryde confirmation (vacancy G3), so the band record remains probative corroboration of the AYE crawl the driver described.

flag_account under RD-6 requires RD-2 refund > 0 or a recorded RD-1 violation, and the rider's own brief yields only $1.13 on one segment; meanwhile F16 shows 1 upheld dispute with 0 route deviations upheld in 90 days, so there is no 'repeated' route-deviation pattern to refer.
